# Beacons, flag codes and heliograph (`signal_beacons_flag_codes`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/communication.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Communication & information (`communication`)
- Deps: helped by glass_mirrors, telescope
- Core idea: Visual signals over long distances: fire by night, smoke by day, flags or mirrors. A chain of beacons on hilltops passes a single agreed message ('the enemy is coming') hundreds of kilometres in an hour. To send any message you need a code: Polybius' torch code lays the alphabet in a 5 x 5 grid and shows the row and column by numbers of torches; naval codes give each flag a digit and each number a word or sentence in a codebook (Popham, 1800). The heliograph flashes sunlight from a mirror in Morse code over 50 km or more.
- Pitfalls:
  - A beacon chain sends only what was agreed in advance; a false alarm cannot be called back
  - Spelling out messages letter by letter: use a codebook of words and phrases
  - Forgetting that the enemy can see and read the signals
  - Weather and night stop flags and heliographs
- History: mesopotamia: c. 1780 BC – letters from Mari report fire signals between towns; greece: 458 BC – Aeschylus' Agamemnon describes a beacon chain from Troy (literary); c. 350 BC Aeneas Tacticus' synchronised water-vessel signal; 2nd c. BC Polybius (Histories X.43–47) describes his torch alphabet; china: Han – frontier beacon towers (fengsui) with written rules on the number of fires and smokes for each kind of incursion (Juyan documents); rome: signal towers along frontiers and coasts; europe: 1588 – English beacon chain warns of the Armada; 1800 Popham's numerical flag code; 1857 British Commercial Code of Signals, later the International Code of Signals; 1869 Mance's heliograph; americas: 1860 – Myer's wig-wag flag signalling for the US Army; Plains peoples' smoke signals; india: 1870s – heliographs used on the North-West Frontier and in Afghanistan
- Read:
  - Polybius, Histories X.43–47 (2nd c. BC)
  - Gerard J. Holzmann & Björn Pehrson, The Early History of Data Networks (1995)
